short: What the stocks and crypto you own are worth today.
detail: The value today of the stocks and crypto you own. It goes up and down as their prices change, so it can be more or less than the money you put in.
example: 3 shares at a closing price of $20 each are $60 invested.

short: A small piece of a company that you can own.
detail: When the company does well, its stock can grow. It can also drop fast. That is why a stock's price goes up and down.
example: Owning one share of Apple means you own a tiny piece of Apple.

short: One unit of a company's stock that you can buy or sell.
detail: Each share has a price. When the price goes up, every share you own is worth more. You can also own part of a share.
example: If one share costs $50 and you own 2 shares, you have $100.

short: Digital money that no government or bank runs.
detail: It lives on a network of computers. Its price can swing a lot in a single day. It trades every day, even on weekends.
example: Bitcoin and Ethereum are two kinds of crypto.

short: A small payment some companies make to the people who own their stock.
detail: A company can share part of what it earns with its owners. It pays a set amount for each share you owned before a certain date. In First Leaf, the payment lands in your cash.
example: A company pays 27 cents a share. If you own 2 shares, you get 54 cents.

short: The date that decides who gets the next dividend.
detail: A company sets this date for each dividend it pays. If you own a share before that date, you get the payment. If you buy on or after it, you wait for the next one.
example: Say the date is Nov. 10. You must own the share by Nov. 9 to get that payment.

short: How much an investment's price tends to jump around.
detail: We rate each one from 1, calm, to 5, bumpy, using how much its price moved each day over the past year. Bumpy ones can grow more over time, but they can also fall more on a bad day.
example: Costco is a 1. Solana is a 5.

source.label: Investor.gov: Assessing your risk tolerance (U.S. SEC)

short: When your money earns money, and then that new money earns money too.
detail: It starts small and speeds up over time, like a snowball rolling downhill. The more years it has, the bigger it gets.
example: $100 that grows 6% becomes $106. The next year, the 6% is on $106, not $100.

short: How much your money grew or shrank, shown as a percent.
detail: A percent makes it easy to compare big and small amounts. A 5% return on $100 is $5. A 5% return on $1,000 is $50.
example: Up $5 on $100 is a 5% rate of return.

short: Buying the same dollar amount on a set schedule, whatever the price.
detail: When prices are low, the same dollars buy more shares. When prices are high, they buy fewer. Auto-invest does this with each monthly deposit.
example: $150 on the first of each month buys more shares in a month when prices dipped.

short: An order to buy or sell right away at the current price.
detail: It fills fast, but the price can be a little different from the last price you saw. Practice fills each order at the latest price.
example: A market order for $50 of a stock buys $50 of it at the current price.

short: The short wait after you buy or sell before the trade is final.
detail: In the U.S., most trades are final one business day later. Until then, the trade shows as settling.
example: You buy on Monday. It is final on Tuesday.

source.label: Investor.gov: New T+1 settlement cycle (U.S. SEC)

short: An account you use to buy, sell and hold stocks and other investments.
detail: A brokerage holds your investments and your cash for you. Your First Leaf starter account is a brokerage account.
example: You put money into your brokerage account, then buy shares with it.

source.label: Investor.gov: Opening a brokerage account (U.S. SEC)

short: The person you choose to get your account if you die.
detail: You name them ahead of time. Then the money can go to them with fewer steps for your family. You can change who it is at any time.
example: Rosa can name her brother. If she dies, her account goes to him.

short: Protection for stocks and cash at a member brokerage that fails.
detail: SIPC protection covers stocks and cash at a member brokerage if the brokerage fails. It doesn't cover crypto, such as Bitcoin or Ethereum. It never covers a drop in price.
example: If a member brokerage closed and shares went missing, SIPC would work to get them back to their owners.
